lead: A car must show its size and intention to other road users, and light the road for its driver. Lamps are grouped by function: front, rear, interior and special purpose. Each group has a beam pattern, colour rule, switch and legal limit. Only a few universities teach this grouping in depth; the electrical content is the same circuit path — battery, fuse, switch or relay, lamp, earth. You meet it when a Chennai bus flashes its hazard lamps at a breakdown.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.5 for lamp types, ratings and efficacy.

blocks.text: Front lamps do two jobs: light the road and signal. Headlamps have main beam (high beam) for empty roads and dip beam (low beam) for traffic. Dip beam is aimed down and left in India, giving an asymmetric cut-off: the near kerb is lit, the oncoming driver is not dazzled. Aiming screws or a motor set the beam; see Chapter 2.7. The dip cut-off is checked at a test lane; a high aim fails the inspection.

Daytime running lamps (DRLs) are low-power white lamps that switch on with the engine. Fog lamps are wide and low for mist; front fog lamps are white or selective yellow. Position lamps mark the car's width at night. To the front, lamps are white or amber, and the only amber lamps at the front are the direction indicators. A relay is used because two 55 W headlamps draw about 9.2 A at 12 V, too much for a small dash switch. This is why a headlamp relay clicks when you switch on.

Rear lamps signal from behind. Tail lamps are red and come on with the position lamps. Stop lamps are brighter red and work only when the brake pedal closes its switch; a typical stop lamp is 21 W. Reversing lamps are white and switch on with reverse gear. Direction indicators are amber and flash at about 90 per minute. Rear fog lamps are red and much brighter than tail lamps; use them only in poor visibility. The number-plate lamp is white and lights the plate without glare.

Interior lamps are convenience loads: dome, map, vanity, ambient, boot and glovebox lamps. Many use a door switch to earth, so opening a door completes the circuit. Dimming uses pulse-width modulation (PWM): a switch turns the lamp on and off quickly, and the eye sees average brightness. All these lamps return to the body earth. A failed earth makes several lamps glow dimly through each other.

Special lamps warn or work. Hazard warning lamps flash all four indicators; the hazard switch has its own supply so it works with the ignition off. Beacons and flashing lamps on ambulances, police and maintenance vehicles use a separate flasher or LED driver. Work lamps on trucks and tractors are white and aimed at the job. School-bus lamps include red flashing warning lamps and a stop-arm lamp.

The circuit path is fixed: battery → fuse → lighting switch → relay for high current → lamp → earth return (figure). The fuse protects the wiring, not the lamp. The flasher unit is a thermal or electronic switch that opens and closes the indicator circuit; it sets the flash rate and blinks the dash tell-tale. Electric horns sit on the same auxiliary family: battery, fuse, relay and horn, switched by the horn button. Front and rear lamps are in parallel, so one failure does not stop the others, and the total current adds.

examples.question: Two 55 W headlamps, two 5 W tail lamps, two 5 W number-plate lamps and 3 W of instrument illumination are on together. The battery is at 12.6 V. Find total current and choose the next standard fuse above it with margin.
steps: The next standard fuse above 10.6 A with margin is 15 A; it carries the load and protects the wiring.
examples.answer: Total current is 10.6 A, and a 15 A fuse is chosen.
examples.check:
P = 2*55 + 2*5 + 2*5 + 3
V = 12.6
I = P / V
print(P)
print(round(I, 1))
print(15)

traps: Using 12 V when the alternator charges at 13.8–14.4 V gives a current that is too low; two 55 W/12 V headlamps draw about 9.2 A at 12 V but about 11 A at 14.4 V because lamp current rises with supply voltage.
Forgetting that brake lamps add 42 W only when the pedal is pressed.
Swapping main and dip beam: main beam has no asymmetric cut-off.
Putting a white lamp at the rear or a red lamp at the front; colour rules are legal.
Treating the flasher unit as a fuse; it sets the 90 per minute rate.

quiz.a: Dash switch carries small current; relay contacts carry 9.2 A.

quiz.q: Two 55 W headlamps rated at 12 V run at 13.8 V: current? (Each lamp R = 2.62 Ω.)
quiz.a: R per lamp = 12² ÷ 55 = 2.62 Ω; I per lamp = 13.8 ÷ 2.62 = 5.27 A; total 10.5 A.

quiz.q: Why does the hazard switch have a permanent supply?
quiz.a: Hazards must work with ignition off, e.g. at a breakdown.

quiz.q: Why is the number-plate lamp white?
quiz.a: It must make the plate readable; red would hide characters.

quiz.q: A 21 W stop lamp at 12 V: current?

beyond: Not for the exam. New cars use LED matrix headlamps that switch individual pixels to shape the beam, and OLED rear lamps that are thin panels. Regulations still decide colour, aim and flash rate, so electronics changes the lamp, not the rule. Search for matrix beam, PWM dimming and vehicle lighting installation standards if you want the circuits and rules. The next step is adaptive lighting in Chapter 2.7.
